summaries.example: Imagine a puzzle made of many pieces. Each piece is one thing, but it also has smaller parts. Al-Kindi asked whether there must be a special source that explains how things can be both one thing and made of many parts. He called this source the “true One,” meaning God.
summaries.summary:
Al-Kindi lived around the ninth century. He was born in Basra and educated in Baghdad, and he worked near the Abbasid court. He is often described as the first person in the Arabic tradition to call himself a philosopher. He helped lead a circle of translators who turned Greek works about philosophy, mathematics, and science into Arabic. Al-Kindi then used these ideas in his own writings.

His most famous philosophical work, On First Philosophy, links the study of truth with the study of God. Al-Kindi says that everything in the world has some kind of unity, even though things also contain many parts. He argues that this unity needs a source that is completely one. He calls this source the “true One.” He also says that God brings beings into existence from non-being and that the world is not without a beginning. The source describes his arguments and also notes that some of them are open to criticism.

Al-Kindi taught that the rational soul is not the same as the body. He described different states of the intellect, including the ability to think and the activity of thinking. He also explained dreams using the imagination, the brain, and the soul. In ethics, he advised people not to place their deepest hopes in possessions, because possessions can be lost and do not last forever.

Al-Kindi used mathematics in areas such as optics and music. He also wrote about medicine, weather, the heavens, and astrology. His lasting importance comes partly from his own ideas and partly from helping make Greek philosophy available for later Arabic, Jewish, and Latin thinkers.
key_ideas: Al-Kindi was an important early philosopher who wrote in Arabic and helped connect Greek learning with the Muslim world of his time.
He helped organize translators who brought works by Aristotle, Plotinus, Proclus, Euclid, Ptolemy, and others into Arabic.
He argued that the world had a beginning and that God is the completely one source of being and unity.
He wrote about the soul, thinking, dreams, mathematics, medicine, music, optics, astrology, and the heavens.
His work helped create words and methods for discussing philosophy in Arabic.
summaries.why_it_matters: Al-Kindi shows how knowledge can travel between languages and cultures. He did not simply repeat Greek thinkers. He combined their ideas with questions important in his own Muslim society. His work helped develop Arabic philosophical vocabulary and influenced later discussions of God, the soul, science, and knowledge. Studying him also shows that philosophy can connect with mathematics, medicine, religion, and the study of nature.

important_terms.definition: A thinker who asks careful questions about truth, knowledge, reality, and how people should live.
The study of the deepest questions about reality, God, being, and what things are.
A way of thinking about God as completely one, without separate parts or qualities that would make God divided.
The study of the soul, thinking, feeling, and the powers of the mind.
The power to think about ideas, rather than only seeing or touching things.

summaries.summary:
Abu Yusuf Ya‘qub ibn Ishaq al-Kindi, usually dated to about 800–870 CE, was a major ninth-century intellectual associated with Basra, Baghdad, and the Abbasid court. He is often called the first self-described philosopher in the Arabic tradition. He helped supervise a leading translation circle, whose members rendered Greek philosophical and scientific works into Arabic. The surviving record attributes hundreds of treatises to him, although many are lost. His writings range across philosophy, mathematics, medicine, music, optics, cosmology, and astrology.

Al-Kindi’s central philosophical work, On First Philosophy, treats metaphysics as knowledge of the first truth: God. Its argument about divine unity begins with an analysis of ordinary things and their predicates. Genus, species, individuals, and their features each display both unity and multiplicity. Al-Kindi argues that this combination cannot explain itself and cannot be due merely to chance. It therefore requires an external cause that is one in itself, not merely one among many. This “true One” is God. Because ordinary predicates imply multiplicity, al-Kindi concludes that they cannot straightforwardly describe God; the divine nature is radically simple.

Al-Kindi also presents God as an efficient cause who brings beings from non-being. He denies that this act requires a preexisting subject or elapsed time. In arguing that the world is not eternal, he draws especially on John Philoponus while using considerations related to Aristotle’s treatment of infinity. The SEP account emphasizes that the argument’s success is uncertain, since an eternal world might involve only a potentially infinite series rather than an actually infinite total existing at once.

key_ideas: Al-Kindi’s philosophical project combines Aristotelian, Neoplatonic, mathematical, and contemporary theological materials rather than following one source without alteration.
He identifies first philosophy with knowledge of God, because God is the first truth and the cause of being and truth.
His argument for the “true One” begins from the claim that ordinary things combine unity and multiplicity; their unity therefore requires an external, purely one cause.
Al-Kindi treats creation as God’s bringing being from non-being without requiring a material subject or a period of time for the creative act.
His psychology is strongly dualist and intellectualist: rational thought is treated as distinct from sensation, and the intellect is activated by an external intelligible source.
His scientific work emphasizes mathematical explanation, while his cosmology explains earthly processes through the causal influence of the heavens.
summaries.why_it_matters: Al-Kindi is important for the history of philosophy because he helped establish a philosophical vocabulary and method in Arabic. His work illustrates how translation can become creative interpretation: Aristotle and Neoplatonic authors supplied major resources, while Islamic theology and Arabic intellectual disciplines shaped the questions being addressed. His theories also connect metaphysics with psychology, ethics, cosmology, and mathematical science. Later Arabic, Jewish, and Latin thinkers inherited parts of this project, even when they did not agree with al-Kindi or cite him directly.

important_terms.definition: The branch of philosophy concerned with being, reality, causation, God, and the basic structure of the world.
The view that God is wholly one and does not have distinct parts or attributes that would introduce multiplicity into the divine nature.
A cause that produces an effect or brings something into existence, as opposed to a final cause, which explains what an effect is directed toward.
An infinity that exists as a completed whole, rather than as a process that can be extended or divided without a final limit.
A non-material principle or form of life and thought; in al-Kindi’s psychology, the rational soul is distinct from the body.
The capacity for intellectual understanding; al-Kindi describes it through states including potential, actual, and acquired intellect.
A philosophical view that explains knowledge primarily through intellectual activity rather than deriving intellectual forms from sense experience.
The study of the heavens and their effects on the earthly world; al-Kindi presented astrology as a rational causal discipline.

summaries.example: Suppose your class has a team project. The team is one group, but it contains many students, jobs, and ideas. Al-Kindi might ask: what explains the team’s being one group at all? He argued that ordinary things are often both one and many, so their unity cannot be explained only by another ordinary thing. He proposed a source that is one in a deeper sense—the “true One,” or God.
summaries.summary:
Al-Kindi was a scholar who lived in the ninth century, probably from about 800 to 870 CE. He was born in Basra, studied in Baghdad, and became connected with the Abbasid court. Later writers called him the “philosopher of the Arabs,” and he is often described as the first philosopher in the Arabic tradition to identify himself that way.

Al-Kindi worked with translators who brought Greek works into Arabic. These included writings connected with Aristotle, Neoplatonism, mathematics, and science. He was influenced most strongly by Aristotle, but he also used ideas linked to Plotinus, Proclus, and John Philoponus. Rather than treating these sources as completely separate, he tried to show how they could support one broad philosophical picture. He also used philosophy to discuss questions important in his Muslim setting.

In metaphysics, Al-Kindi connects “first philosophy” with knowledge of God. He argues that things in the world are both one and many. A person is one individual but has many parts; a species is one kind but includes many individuals. Al-Kindi says this mixture needs a cause that is one in a stronger sense. He calls it the “true One.” Since ordinary qualities and categories involve multiplicity, he argues that they cannot describe God as they describe created things. This is his account of divine simplicity.

Al-Kindi also says God creates beings from non-being and that the world is not eternal. His arguments draw on Philoponus’s criticisms of Aristotle, especially about infinity. However, the SEP entry explains that critics may distinguish an actual infinite from a process that can continue without limit, creating a challenge for Al-Kindi’s reasoning.

key_ideas: Al-Kindi helped bring Greek philosophy and science into Arabic through a ninth-century translation movement.
He combined ideas from Aristotle and Neoplatonic writers, while also responding to questions in Islamic theology.
He argued that God is the “true One,” the source of unity and being, and that ordinary descriptions do not apply to God in the same way.
He defended the view that the world was created and is not infinitely old, although the source explains that his argument can be questioned.
He described the rational soul and intellect as distinct from ordinary bodily sensation, and he connected this view with dreams and ethics.
He used mathematics to study subjects such as optics, music, medicine, and the workings of the heavens.
summaries.why_it_matters: Al-Kindi’s story matters because it shows that philosophy grows through conversation across languages, religions, and regions. He helped create Arabic terms for Greek philosophical ideas, but he also changed those ideas while applying them to new questions. His work connects abstract arguments about God and creation with practical subjects such as sadness, dreams, medicine, mathematics, and the stars. It also helps explain how later philosophers in Arabic, Jewish, and Latin traditions received ancient Greek thought.

important_terms.definition: A person who studies big questions about reality, knowledge, God, and how people should live.
The study of what is most real and what lies behind the things we experience.
The idea that God is completely one and is not made of separate parts or independent qualities.
The study of the soul and the ways living beings think, imagine, and act.
The ability to understand ideas and reasons, not just information received through the senses.
A philosophical disagreement about whether the universe has always existed or began at a particular point.
The study of the heavens and how heavenly bodies may affect events on Earth.

Why might a philosopher think that a cause must be outside a chain of things that are both one and many?
What is gained, and what might be lost, when ideas from different cultures are combined?
